CURRENT SITUATION — day 76

memory_block.body: 40% SMB discount: signup +31%, rev +18%, ret -12% at renewal; sugar high, don't generalize. Measured in the standard SMB segment.
Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.

answer.rationale:
The two degraded metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and onboarding is upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly recovers both. Two inherited memories converge on it (memory_86 shortened onboarding, memory_31 cut signup fields), which is why I intend simplify_onboarding rather than activation_messaging (memory_91 is a narrower, downstream nudge). I am deliberately NOT choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is the one inherited record with actual numbers and it says the discount bought signups (+31%) and short-term revenue (+18%) while costing retention (-12%) at renewal — that is a direct trade against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and the competitor pressure is exactly the condition that makes the 'sugar high' tempting. Referral incentive (memory_57) is credible but addresses established customers, not the failing stage; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and does not touch the QoQ declines.

I am spending both verification pulls on the memories that actually carry my decision, memory_86 and memory_31, because both are stated qualitatively with no effect size, no segment, no sample, and no durability window — 'lifting early product adoption' could be a 0.5% blip. memory_31 is also 64 days old and memory_86 24 days old; the funnel they were measured on may not be the current funnel, and the current declines may indicate the product changed underneath them. I want the original records to check effect size, whether the lift persisted past week one, and whether either was measured on the same self-serve segment now degrading. I am not verifying memory_73 even though it is decision-relevant, because it already carries explicit numbers and an explicit scope caveat, so re-reading it would buy less than checking the two vague claims I am about to act on.

Downstream value risk: cutting required signup fields and shortening onboarding can lift completion while degrading the data used for lead scoring, routing, and enterprise qualification — i.e. it can raise the top-line count of activated accounts while lowering the qualified fraction, which would look like a win on the experiment metric and a loss on the actual objective. memory_31 measures activation, not revenue quality, so it cannot rule this out. Guardrails: hold out a control, instrument qualified-pipeline-per-signup and 30/60-day retention as co-primary metrics rather than completion rate alone, and do not remove fields that feed enterprise routing (memory_44 indicates that path is where pipeline quality lives). Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, since the supporting evidence is unquantified; if verification returns thin or stale records I will drop to a small guarded test on a single self-serve cohort instead of committing the full slot.
